procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chingleput
procedural_history.impugned_order: Notification of the village as a zamindari estate under the Act, which the respondent claimed was illegal and void.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text does not explicitly state what the High Court did. However, since the State is appealing to the Supreme Court, it can be inferred that the Subordinate Judge ruled in favor of Govindarajulu, and the State appealed to the High Court, which affirmed the Subordinate Judge's decision.

directions: The appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the village, which was included in the assets of the zamindari at the time of the permanent settlement, was part of the zamindari estate.

facts: The appellant contended that because the village was included in the assets of the zamindari at the time of the permanent settlement, it was legally part of the zamindari estate.
law: Under the Madras Estates Land Act (s. 3(2)(e)), a village held on a 'permanent under-tenure' is considered a separate 'estate'.
Permanent under-tenure villages are specifically excluded from the definition of a 'zamin estate' under the relevant Act.

To constitute an under-tenure, the key factor is that the reversionary interest rests with the proprietor of the zamindari, which can happen if the inam was included in the zamindari's assets at the permanent settlement.
application: The Court explained that when a pre-existing inam village was included in the assets of a zamindari during the permanent settlement, the legal effect was not to merge the village into the zamindari.
Instead, this created a situation where the inamdar, who previously held the village under the Government, now held it as a 'permanent under-tenure' under the zamindar.
The zamindar became an intermediary between the inamdar and the Government.
The Court cited two previous Madras High Court decisions which held that when a pre-settlement village was included in the assets of a zamindari, it became a permanent under-tenure.
Therefore, the fact that the village was included in the zamindari's assets is what established it as an under-tenure, a distinct legal category.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the inclusion of the village in the zamindari's assets at the time of the permanent settlement did not make it part of the zamindari estate. Instead, this action legally established the village as a 'permanent under-tenure,' which is a separate type of estate and is excluded from the definition of a 'zamin estate'.

issue.issue_text: Whether the village, being held under a permanent under-tenure, falls under the definition of an 'estate' in s. 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.

facts: The case concerned a village that was physically part of a zamindari.
The respondent argued that the village was held on a permanent under-tenure from the zamindar.
The State argued that because the village was included in the assets of the zamindari, it was a 'zamin estate'.
law: Section 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act defines an 'estate' to include "any portion consisting of one or more villages of any of the estates specified in clauses (a), (b) and (c) which is held on a permanent under-tenure."
The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act of 1948 classifies estates defined under s. 3(2)(e) as "under-tenure estates."
This same Act explicitly excludes villages held on a permanent under-tenure from the definition of a "zamin estate."
application: The Court established that the crucial factor for a village to be an under-tenure is not whether the grant was made before or after the permanent settlement, but that it is held permanently from a superior landlord (the zamindar) who holds the reversionary interest.

The Court applied the law directly, stating that even if a village is physically part of a zamindari, its legal status as a permanent under-tenure brings it under the specific definition of an 'estate' in s. 3(2)(e).
By falling under s. 3(2)(e), the village is legally classified as an "under-tenure estate."
The Court emphasized that the legal framework creates a clear distinction: an under-tenure estate is specifically excluded from the definition of a zamin estate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the village was held under a permanent under-tenure, it squarely fell under the definition of an 'estate' in Section 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act. Consequently, it was an 'under-tenure estate' and not a 'zamin estate'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the village, which was included in the assets of the zamindari at the time of the permanent settlement, was part of the zamindari estate.
appellant_arguments: The village was included in the assets of the zamindari at the time of the permanent settlement and was therefore part of the zamindari.
The Chingleput Manual lists the village under the heading 'Zamindaries' and not under 'inam villages', which supports the claim that it was part of the zamindari.
respondent_arguments: Although the village was included in the assets of the zamindari, its pre-existing tenure as a shrotriem grant was not disturbed by the permanent settlement.
The grantee and his successors continued to hold the village as an under-tenure from the zamindar, who had become an intermediary.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the village, being held under a permanent under-tenure, falls under the definition of an 'estate' in s. 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
appellant_arguments: A document showed that the holder of the village was only a lessee for 10 years, not a permanent tenure holder.
The village was a part of the zamindari estate itself, not a separate under-tenure estate.
respondent_arguments: The village was an under-tenure estate falling under the definition in s. 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
The village was granted as a shrotriem before the permanent settlement, and this pre-existing tenure continued undisturbed, making it a permanent under-tenure.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A village held under a permanent under-tenure falls within the definition of an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
obiter: No presumption can be drawn from an unsigned statement that does not bear a date.
Zamindars are entitled, according to usage, to call upon the inhabitants of shrotriem lands for assistance for customary purposes.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: As the village is held under a permanent under-tenure, it falls squarely under the definition of s. 3 (2 )( e) of the Madras Estates Land Act and is, therefore, an estate thereunder and hence it is an under-tenure estate. As the under-tenure estate is excluded from the definition of "zamin estate", the notification issued by the Government on the basis that it is a zamin estate is void and the High Court rightly declared it as void.
legal_tests_applied: Definition of 'estate' under s. 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
Definition of 'zamin estate' under the relevant Act, which excludes any portion that is itself an estate under s. 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the village was part of the zamindari estate simply because it was included in its assets at the time of the permanent settlement was incorrect; the court found that the pre-existing shrotriem tenure continued as a permanent under-tenure.
The government's notification was based on the incorrect legal classification of the village as a 'zamin estate', when it was actually an 'under-tenure estate'.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the village was held under a permanent under-tenure, which pre-dated the permanent settlement.
Because the village was a permanent under-tenure, it qualified as an 'estate' under the specific definition in s. 3(2)(e) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
As an 'under-tenure estate', it was explicitly excluded from the definition of a 'zamin estate', making the government's notification based on that incorrect classification void.
policy_considerations: The court recognized the historical intent to preserve the rights of incumbents holding Shrotriem lands, noting that "length of possession has annexed to them idea of property" even when the administrative offices associated with them were abolished during the permanent settlement.
